title: Does Google Penalize AI Content? No, Only Scaled Low-Value Pages
metaTitle: Does Google Penalize AI Content? Only Scaled Spam
metaDescription: Google does not penalize AI content for being AI. It penalizes scaled, low-value pages. What Google's own pages say, how to stay safe, and what we cut.
shortAnswer: No. Google's guidance says appropriate use of AI is not against its guidelines. What it penalizes is content made primarily to manipulate rankings, including many AI-generated pages that add no value for users, which its spam policy calls scaled content abuse. Violating sites may rank lower or disappear from results. Whether a person or a model typed the draft is not the test; usefulness and scale are.
intro:
Every few months another wave of panic hits content teams: "Google is penalizing AI content." Google's own documentation says something narrower. This page is based on Google Search Central documentation as of 3 October 2026 (its generative AI guidance and helpful-content pages are dated 1 October 2026, its spam policies 28 August 2026).

It covers what Google penalizes, how to use AI without risk, and whether AI engines such as ChatGPT cite AI-written pages.

sections.heading: Does Google penalize AI content?
sections.body:
No. Google's guidance says [appropriate use of AI or automation is not against its guidelines](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2023/02/google-search-and-ai-content), and that it judges the quality of content, not how it was produced. The penalty risk comes from a different thing: publishing pages primarily to manipulate rankings, which Google's spam policy covers whoever or whatever wrote them.

Three statements from Google's own pages settle most of the argument:

- [Using AI gives content no special gains](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2023/02/google-search-and-ai-content): it is "just content", and it may do well if it is useful, helpful, original and shows E-E-A-T.
- Google's [generative AI guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/using-gen-ai-content) says AI can help with research and structure, but using it to generate many pages without adding value for users may violate the spam policy on scaled content abuse.
- Violating sites [may rank lower in results or not appear in results at all](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies).

[E-E-A-T](/glossary/e-e-a-t) stands for experience, expertise, authoritativeness and trustworthiness; Google says [trust is the most important of the four](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content), and that E-E-A-T is not itself a ranking factor.

![Close-up of a robotic hand and a silver-gloved human hand touching](https://images.pexels.com/photos/8849283/pexels-photo-8849283.jpeg?auto=compress&cs=tinysrgb&w=1200)

sections.heading: What does Google actually penalize?
sections.body:
Google penalizes scaled content abuse: many pages generated mainly to manipulate rankings rather than help users, [no matter how they are created](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies). Its examples include generating many pages with AI tools without adding value, scraping and lightly rewording other sites, and stitching sources together with nothing new.

The authorship method is irrelevant to the label. This table shows how we read Google's pages:

| Practice | Policy risk | Why |
|---|---|---|
| AI-drafted article, then fact-checked and given your own data | Low | Appropriate AI use is not against the guidelines |
| Hundreds of AI pages built from a keyword list | High | Named example of scaled content abuse |
| Human-written pages that all say the same thing | High | The policy applies however content is created |
| Scraped, translated or lightly reworded copies | High | Listed as scaled content abuse and as scraping |
| One thin AI page | Not a violation, but weak | Google says it does well only if it is helpful and original |

Google's people-first guidance adds warning signs worth checking against your own site. They include [using extensive automation to produce content on many topics](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content), producing lots of content across topics hoping some performs, and mainly summarizing what others say without adding value.

![Yellow warning signboard under a wooden arch against a blue sky](https://images.pexels.com/photos/6300646/pexels-photo-6300646.jpeg?auto=compress&cs=tinysrgb&w=1200)

sections.heading: Can Google tell that AI wrote a page?
sections.body:
Google has not said it sorts pages by authorship, and it does not need to. It says its systems, including SpamBrain, [analyze patterns and signals to identify spam "however it is produced"](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2023/02/google-search-and-ai-content). In our view, the patterns that matter are thin, repetitive, unoriginal pages, which is what unedited AI output published at volume tends to look like.

That makes "will it detect my AI?" the wrong question. Ask whether a stranger who lands on the page learns something they could not get from the top three results. If the honest answer is no, the page is exposed whether you or a model wrote it.

Human review also exists: Google says violations are found by [automated systems and, as needed, human review that can result in a manual action](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies).

sections.heading: How do you use AI in content safely?
sections.body:
Use AI for research and drafting, then make sure a person adds something the model could not. Fixing grammar is not enough: the edit has to carry your data, your decisions or your disagreement. That is what separates a page from the thousandth near-copy.

1. **Start from something only you have.** First-hand numbers, product usage and screenshots. Google's people-first checklist asks whether content shows [first-hand expertise and depth of knowledge](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content).
2. **Fact-check everything, including the small fields.** Google says generative models predict likely words rather than retrieve facts, so outputs may contain inaccuracies (see [hallucination](/glossary/hallucination)). It says to review titles, meta descriptions, structured data and image alt text too, per its [guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/using-gen-ai-content).
3. **Say how it was made when readers would wonder.** Google says AI or automation disclosures are useful where someone might ask "how was this created?", and that [giving AI an author byline is probably not the best way](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2023/02/google-search-and-ai-content) to do that. For e-commerce, the [guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/using-gen-ai-content) says Merchant Center requires AI-generated product titles and descriptions to be labelled as AI-generated.
4. **Publish fewer, sharper pages.** One intent per page, and nothing off your core topic.
5. **Open every section with the answer.** It reads faster, and it is what AI engines extract. Our [AI for SEO guide](/blog/ai-for-seo) and [guide to optimizing content for AI search](/guides/how-to-optimize-content-for-ai-search) cover the mechanics.

sections.heading: Does AI content get cited by AI engines?
sections.body:
No engine we checked documents a rule for or against AI-written text. What the documents do describe are access gates: [sites opted out of OAI-SearchBot are not shown in ChatGPT search answers](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/bots), and a page can be a supporting link in Google's AI features only if it is [indexed and eligible to show in Search with a snippet](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ai-features). Google adds that no special optimization is needed.

Our reading: a page that Google's spam systems keep out of the index cannot be a supporting link, so the Google penalty risk and the AI-citation risk are largely one problem.

Google also addresses the AI-search angle directly. Its [guide to generative AI features](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/ai-optimization-guide) (updated 10 July 2026) says that making separate content for every query variation or fan-out query, primarily to manipulate rankings or AI responses, violates the scaled content abuse policy. Writing a page per prompt is not a shortcut.

Two research results point in different directions, and neither is a loophole:

- In the GEO paper's benchmark, [adding citations, quotations or statistics improved visibility by 30-40% on one metric and 15-30% on another](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.09735). In our view, unedited drafts usually lack those features.
- A separate lab study found [neural retrievers ranked LLM-generated documents higher](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.20501), which the authors call source bias. It tested research retrieval models, not ChatGPT or Google, so we do not know it carries over, and Google's spam policy sits on top of any such effect.

Our piece on why [most AEO advice is recycled SEO](/blog/most-aeo-advice-is-recycled-seo) makes the same point: the durable work is original, checkable content.

sections.heading: What did we learn from retiring 234 of our own posts?
sections.body:
Volume without readers is dead weight, and we learned it on our own site. On 24 September 2026 we retired 234 of our blog posts and merged 27 duplicates, after Search Console showed about half of our 496 posts were unrelated to AI visibility and had 0 clicks in 90 days.

On 3 October 2026 we merged another 165 pages into 42: 85 duplicate-intent pages into 37 canonical pages, and 80 single-purpose research pages into 5 resource hubs.

Three caveats keep this honest. We received no Google notice that those pages were penalized, we are not claiming they were AI-written, and it is too early to claim our rankings improved. We did it because pages without a reader are a cost.

We stand behind the lesson: one strong page per question beats five thin ones, for Google and for AI retrieval. On the access side, aeoeye.com allows GPTBot, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot, Google-Extended, CCBot and Applebot-Extended in robots.txt, because our business is being found.

keyTakeaways: Google's guidance says appropriate AI use is not against its guidelines; it judges quality, not production method.
The policy risk is scaled content abuse: many pages made mainly to manipulate rankings, however they are created.
Google has not said it sorts pages by authorship; its systems look for spam patterns however content is produced.
Safe use means first-hand material, fact-checking, honest disclosure where readers would wonder, and fewer, sharper pages.
No engine we checked documents a rule about AI-written text, but a page Google excludes cannot be a supporting link in its AI features.

faqs.a: Not for being AI-generated. Google's guidance says appropriate use of AI or automation is not against its guidelines, and that using AI to generate content primarily to manipulate rankings is against its spam policies. The test is purpose and value to the reader. Many low-value AI pages published at scale fall under scaled content abuse; a fact-checked, original AI-assisted page does not.

faqs.q: Does Google have an AI content detector?
faqs.a: Google has not said that it classifies pages by authorship. It says its systems, including SpamBrain, analyze patterns and signals to identify spam however it is produced. In practice, repetitive, thin, unoriginal pages are what get caught, and unedited AI output published at volume tends to look exactly like that.

faqs.q: Should I disclose that AI helped write a page?
faqs.a: Where readers would reasonably wonder how a page was made, yes. Google says AI or automation disclosures are useful in those cases and that giving AI an author byline is probably not the best way to do it. For e-commerce, Google's guidance says Merchant Center requires AI-generated product titles and descriptions to be labelled as AI-generated.

Yes. Google says AI gives content no special gain or penalty: it is just content, and it may do well if it is useful, helpful, original and shows E-E-A-T. Fact-checking, first-hand material and a clear point of view are what make the difference, not whether a model produced the first draft.

faqs.q: Does AI-written content get cited by ChatGPT or Google AI Overviews?
faqs.a: Neither OpenAI nor Google documents a rule about AI-written text. OpenAI says sites opted out of OAI-SearchBot are not shown in ChatGPT search answers; Google says a page needs to be indexed and eligible to show with a snippet to be a supporting link. Citable facts, sources and statistics matter more than who typed the draft.

definitions.definition: Generating many pages primarily to manipulate search rankings rather than help users, however the pages are created, including with generative AI tools.
Experience, expertise, authoritativeness and trustworthiness: the qualities Google's systems look for in helpful content, with trust the most important; not itself a ranking factor.
